rv.q: The last breathless line of the play is “Run!”.
Pickett is a star ascending, and her writing is about to be everywhere on stage and screen: now’s your chance to see where she started.
Tense and original, with a creeping dread, it comes across as a first-rate thriller and a top comedy too.
Her writing is sparky and contemporary.
A minor flaw in a splendid piece of theatre.
By halfway through Lyndsey Turner's slow-boil production, I was wowed by the performances, taken with all the talk, still waiting for the storytelling to go beyond a canter.
One of the great joys of theatre is that sometimes you’re in the room when an extraordinary voice breaks through, when something really quite special happens.
It’s a bold, essential piece of theatre that the West End should always look to have on its stages.
The result is one of the sharpest, funniest and most unsettling pieces of new writing currently on the London stage.
Exceptionally well-acted and taut, 1536 is a thought-provoking and emotionally engrossing experience.
1536 surely heralds a notable theatrical voice across several decades of this century if (at the age of 32 she is also a successful screenwriter) this continues to be Pickett’s chosen form.
This is theatre at its very best.

cn.t: Ava Pickett's acclaimed debut uses Anne Boleyn's fall to explore timeless misogyny through three Essex women, earning near-universal praise for its modern language, brutal relevance, and electrifying performances in this "staggering" West End transfer.
